title: Paul–Wyatt roller-spinning machine
summary: Lewis Paul and John Wyatt patented roller machinery that mechanically spun cotton without fingers, an early mechanized spinning system housed in the first cotton mills.

title: Water-powered cotton spinning at Marvel's Mill
summary: Marvel's Mill operated Paul–Wyatt roller-spinning machinery from 1742 and was the first cotton mill powered by a water wheel.

parents.reason: The mill was built to house and operate the Paul–Wyatt roller-spinning machinery that mechanically spun cotton.
The water wheel supplied the non-human power source that drove the machinery at Marvel's Mill.

title: Integrated cotton production at Cromford
summary: Arkwright's water-powered Cromford mill opened in 1771 with mechanized carding and spinning operations, among the first factories to house both processes. The source does not identify the precise carder installed there.

parents.reason: Arkwright installed water frames at the Cromford mill in 1771 as its powered spinning machinery.

The 1771 Cromford mill housed mechanized carding alongside spinning; this edge records the carding operation as an independent input to its integrated production, without identifying the exact carder design.

title: Arkwright carding engine
summary: Arkwright's patented rotary carding engine converted raw cotton into a continuous lap before spinning, using successively faster rollers and a bobbin-and-flyer mechanism.

parents.reason: Arkwright improved Lewis Paul's 1748 carding machine and patented a rotary carding engine that mechanized preparation of raw cotton before spinning.

title: Mechanized wool carding at Dolobran
summary: A factory at Dolobran near Meifod became the first carding mill in Wales, using mechanized carders to produce yarn for the Welsh flannel industry.

parents.reason: The Dolobran mill used carding machines to open and prepare wool fibers for yarn production.

title: Copperplate printing on textiles
summary: Thomas Bell practiced textile printing from engraved copperplates, an earlier fabric-printing method that his later roller-printing patent sought to make less costly.

title: Multicolor calico printing by rollers
summary: After an improvement associated with Adam Parkinson, Bell's roller machine was successfully used at Bamber Bridge to print calico in two to six colors in one operation.

parents.reason: The Bamber Bridge implementation used Bell's roller-printing machine, with a later improvement allowing multiple colors to print in one operation.

title: Walton's layered carding system
summary: In 1834 James Walton patented a practical carding machine and a new card made of cloth and rubber layers; their combination became standard. Earlier wire-covered card machines had been patented by Lewis Paul in 1748, so this milestone does not claim first wire-card use.

parents.reason: Walton's patented machine and layered cloth-and-rubber card were a specific later carding-machine design, whose combination became standard in the industry.

title: Walton wire-card system in commercial production
summary: The combination of Walton's wire card and layered cloth-and-rubber card became standard in the industry; James Walton & Sons was building it at Haughton Dale from 1857.

parents.reason: The later standard carding system combined Walton's practical wire card with his cloth-and-rubber card covering, and his firm manufactured it from 1857.

title: Pan silver amalgamation
summary: Alvaro Alonso Barba's Potosí process mixed silver ore with salt and mercury, sometimes with copper sulfate, and heated the charge in shallow copper vessels to shorten treatment to hours.

title: Washoe silver-amalgamation process
summary: Developed in the 1860s for Comstock ore, the Washoe variant replaced copper vessels with mechanically agitated iron pans and added grinding by a rotating muller.

parents.reason: The Washoe process was a documented variation of pan amalgamation, retaining mercury, salt, and copper-sulfate treatment while replacing copper vessels with agitated iron pans.

title: Reese River salt-roasting silver process
summary: Introduced in the Reese River district in 1879, this route salt-roasted sulfide ore into silver chloride before recovery in amalgamation pans, treating ores that Washoe processing handled poorly.

parents.reason: The Reese River route retained amalgamation pans for metal recovery, as in the Washoe process, while adding salt-roasting that converted silver sulfides to silver chloride before pan treatment.
